```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::knit_hooks$set(small_mar = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(small_mar = TRUE)

occ <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_occupancy.csv")
counts <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")
reef <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/reef_surveys.csv")

# ridges: the same model with year written three ways
occ$c_year <- occ$year - mean(occ$year)
year_nll <- function(p, x){
  prob <- plogis(p[1] + p[2] * x)
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
}
fit_raw  <- optim(c(0, 0), year_nll, x = occ$year, method = "BFGS")
fit_el   <- optim(c(0, 0), year_nll, x = occ$elapsed, method = "BFGS")
fit_cen  <- optim(c(0, 0), year_nll, x = occ$c_year, method = "BFGS")
cor_of <- function(par, x){
  h <- optimHess(par, year_nll, x = x)
  cov2cor(solve(h))[1, 2]
}
cor_el  <- cor_of(fit_el$par, occ$elapsed)
cor_cen <- cor_of(fit_cen$par, occ$c_year)
true_raw_a <- fit_el$par[1] - fit_el$par[2] * min(occ$year)

# scales: migration against range size and mass, in raw and rescaled units
av <- readRDS("../data/Avonet/AVONET1_BirdLife.rds")
birds <- na.omit(av[, c("Migration", "Range.Size", "Mass")])
birds$migrant <- as.integer(birds$Migration == 3)
mig_nll <- function(p, range, mass){
  prob <- plogis(p[1] + p[2] * range + p[3] * mass)
  -sum(dbinom(birds$migrant, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
}
fit_mig_nm <- optim(c(0, 0, 0), mig_nll, range = birds$Range.Size, mass = birds$Mass)
fit_mig_bfgs_msg <- tryCatch({
  optim(c(0, 0, 0), mig_nll, range = birds$Range.Size, mass = birds$Mass,
        method = "BFGS")
  "no error"
}, error = function(e){ conditionMessage(e) })
fit_mig_sc <- optim(c(0, 0, 0), mig_nll, range = birds$Range.Size / 1e6,
                    mass = birds$Mass / 1000, method = "BFGS")
fit_mig_sc_nm <- optim(c(0, 0, 0), mig_nll, range = birds$Range.Size / 1e6,
                       mass = birds$Mass / 1000)

# keeping parameters legal: the reef hump from one sensible-looking start
hump_nat <- function(p){
  mu <- p[1] * exp(-(reef$depth - p[2])^2 / (2 * p[3]^2))
  -sum(dnbinom(reef$richness, mu = mu, size = p[4], log = TRUE))
}
hump_log <- function(p){
  mu <- exp(p[1]) * exp(-(reef$depth - p[2])^2 / (2 * exp(p[3])^2))
  -sum(dnbinom(reef$richness, mu = mu, size = exp(p[4]), log = TRUE))
}
hump_pen <- function(p){
  if (any(p[c(1, 3, 4)] <= 0)) { return(1e10) }
  hump_nat(p)
}
h_start <- c(25, 10, 20, 0.2)
h_warn <- 0
h_nat <- withCallingHandlers(optim(h_start, hump_nat, method = "BFGS"),
                             warning = function(w){
                               h_warn <<- h_warn + 1
                               invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
                             })
h_log <- optim(c(log(25), 10, log(20), log(0.2)), hump_log, method = "BFGS")
h_bnd <- optim(h_start, hump_nat, method = "L-BFGS-B",
               lower = c(0.01, 0, 0.1, 0.01))
h_pen_bfgs <- optim(h_start, hump_pen, method = "BFGS")
h_pen_nm <- optim(h_start, hump_pen)

# errors in a loop: the unguarded straight line from Lecture 16
lin_nll <- function(p){
  prob <- p[1] + p[2] * occ$elapsed
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
}
set.seed(20)
loop_res <- rep(NA, 10)
for (i in 1:10) {
  start <- c(runif(1, 0.5, 1), runif(1, -0.03, 0.01))
  loop_res[i] <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(optim(start, lin_nll, method = "BFGS"))$value,
                          error = function(e){ NA })
}
first_error <- which(is.na(loop_res))[1]

# starting values: build up from the simpler model
plain_nll <- function(p){
  mu <- exp(p[1] + p[2] * counts$frac_built)
  -sum(dnbinom(counts$count, mu = mu, size = exp(p[3]), log = TRUE))
}
threshold_nll <- function(p){
  mu <- exp(p[1] + p[2] * pmax(0, counts$frac_built - p[3]))
  -sum(dnbinom(counts$count, mu = mu, size = exp(p[4]), log = TRUE))
}
fit_plain <- optim(c(2, -1, 0), plain_nll)
fit_built <- optim(c(fit_plain$par[1:2], 0, fit_plain$par[3]), threshold_nll)
fit_tuesday <- optim(c(2, -1, 0.3, 0), threshold_nll)

# the fix-it challenge
bad_nll <- function(p, depth = reef$depth, vis = reef$visibility, yr = reef$year){
  mu <- exp(p[1] + p[2] * depth + p[3] * depth^2 + p[4] * vis + p[5] * yr)
  -sum(dnbinom(reef$richness, mu = mu, size = p[6], log = TRUE))
}
fx_start <- c(3, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1)
fx_try <- function(...){
  suppressWarnings(optim(fx_start, bad_nll, method = "BFGS", ...))$value
}
fx_raw    <- fx_try()
fx_nm     <- suppressWarnings(optim(fx_start, bad_nll))$value
fx_center <- fx_try(yr = reef$year - mean(reef$year))
fx_scale  <- fx_try(depth = reef$depth / 10, vis = reef$visibility / 10)
fx_both   <- fx_try(depth = reef$depth / 10, vis = reef$visibility / 10,
                    yr = reef$year - mean(reef$year))
fx_glm    <- -as.numeric(logLik(MASS::glm.nb(richness ~ depth + I(depth^2) +
                                               visibility + year, data = reef)))
```

## Today's agenda {.smaller}

- Tuesday: how to **notice** a fit that went wrong
- Today: how to **fix** it
- Four fixes: **centering**, **rescaling**, **keeping parameters legal**, and
  **good starting values**
- Plus: how to keep **one failed fit** from stopping a whole loop
- A challenge: **fix a broken model**

. . .

[Type and run]{.type-badge} on a code block: type it into your script and run it.
Code without the label is there to watch.

::: {.notes}
Bolker 7.4. Tuesday was diagnosis: false bottoms, plateaus, multiple starts,
drawing the fit. Today is treatment. Every fix today is a change to how the model
is written, not to what it means: the same biology, re-expressed so the optimizer
can find its answer.
:::

## The story so far {.smaller}

- An optimizer **searches** for the bottom of the NLL surface
- It can stop in the **wrong place** and still report `convergence = 0`
- **Today:** the four most common reasons, and the fix for each

::: {.notes}
Thirty seconds. The callback worth making: Tuesday's table said "re-parameterize
(Thursday)" for ridges. This is Thursday.
:::

## Get set up {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(biometrydata)

occ <- bobwhite_occupancy
counts <- bobwhite_counts
reef <- reef_surveys

# bird traits: keep the columns we need, and drop species missing any of them
birds <- avonet[, c("Migration", "Range.Size", "Mass")]
birds <- na.omit(birds)
birds$migrant <- as.integer(birds$Migration == 3)    # 1 = long-distance migrant
```
:::

Four datasets you know: occupancy by year, counts by route, reef surveys, and
AVONET's bird traits.

::: {.notes}
Nothing new; every dataset today is one they have used before. That is
deliberate: the point is that a model they already understand can still fail to
fit, for reasons that have nothing to do with the biology.

AVONET codes Migration as 1 (sedentary), 2 (partial migrant) and 3 (full
migrant). The last line turns that into a 0/1 response for a binomial model,
which is used in Fix 2.
:::

# Fix 1: center your covariates

## Same model, three ways to write the year {.smaller}

The occupancy model, $p = \text{logistic}(a + b \cdot \text{year})$, with "year"
written three ways:

| Year as | $a$ means | Correlation of $a$ and $b$ | BFGS from (0, 0) |
|---|---|---|---|
| calendar year, 1997 to 2019 | occupancy in **year 0 AD** | effectively $-1$ | NLL **`r round(fit_raw$value, 1)`**, `convergence` `r fit_raw$convergence` |
| years since 1997 | occupancy in 1997 | `r round(cor_el, 2)` | NLL `r round(fit_el$value, 2)` |
| years from the middle year | occupancy in the **middle** year (`r mean(occ$year)`) | `r round(cor_cen, 2)` | NLL `r round(fit_cen$value, 2)` |

. . .

**Same model. Same data.** With the calendar year, BFGS stops far from the bottom
and reports success.

::: {.notes}
The right answer is NLL 56.69 in every row: these are three ways of writing one
model. Only the first fails, and it fails silently.

Why the calendar year is a ridge: a is the log odds of occupancy in year 0, two
thousand years before the data. Any small change in the slope b swings that
far-off intercept by a huge amount, so a and b can only move together, along a
valley so narrow it is nearly a line. Their correlation is so close to -1 that R
cannot even compute it.

Years since 1997 helps a lot (the intercept is now at the edge of the data), and
centering on the middle year helps most: a is then the occupancy in a typical
year, and it barely depends on the slope at all.
:::

## Your turn: break it {background-color="#f0f4f8" .bigcode}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
year_nll <- function(p, x){
  prob <- plogis(p[1] + p[2] * x)
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes,
              prob = prob, log = TRUE))
}

# the calendar year, as it comes in the data
fit_raw <- optim(c(0, 0), year_nll, x = occ$year,
                 method = "BFGS")
fit_raw$value
fit_raw$convergence
```
:::

**Check:** an NLL of `r round(fit_raw$value, 1)`, with `convergence` `r fit_raw$convergence`.
The bottom is at `r round(fit_cen$value, 2)`.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The function now takes the covariate as a second argument, x, so
the same NLL can be fitted to any version of year; optim() passes x = ... through
to it.

Let them sit with the result for a moment: the fit reports success, and it is
nearly 40 units from the bottom.
:::

## Your turn: fix it {background-color="#f0f4f8" .bigcode}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# centered: subtract the mean year
occ$c_year <- occ$year - mean(occ$year)

fit_cen <- optim(c(0, 0), year_nll, x = occ$c_year,
                 method = "BFGS")
fit_cen$value
fit_cen$convergence
fit_cen$par
```
:::

**Check:** `r round(fit_cen$value, 2)`, the true bottom, and a slope $b$ of
`r round(fit_cen$par[2], 3)`, the same as Lecture 16's.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. One new line, and the same function.

The slope b comes out the same as in Lecture 16, -0.062: centering changes what
a means, not what b means. That is the general rule, and it is why centering is
free.
:::

## Why centering works {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 8.4
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.4, 3.6, 1.8, 0.6), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0))
b_seq <- seq(-0.1, -0.025, length.out = 100)
a_raw <- seq(true_raw_a - 80, true_raw_a + 80, length.out = 100)
z_raw <- outer(a_raw, b_seq, Vectorize(function(a, b){ year_nll(c(a, b), occ$year) }))
contour(a_raw, b_seq, log(z_raw - min(z_raw) + 1), nlevels = 10,
        drawlabels = FALSE, xlab = "a (year 0)", ylab = "b", main = "calendar year")
a_cen <- seq(fit_cen$par[1] - 0.4, fit_cen$par[1] + 0.4, length.out = 100)
z_cen <- outer(a_cen, b_seq, Vectorize(function(a, b){ year_nll(c(a, b), occ$c_year) }))
contour(a_cen, b_seq, log(z_cen - min(z_cen) + 1), nlevels = 10,
        drawlabels = FALSE, xlab = "a (middle year)", ylab = "b", main = "centered year")
```

Left: a valley so narrow it is almost a line. Right: a round bowl.

::: {.plain}
Measure from the middle of your data, not from zero. The intercept then describes a year you actually observed, instead of a wild extrapolation two thousand years back, and the optimizer can find it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Both panels are the same surface, drawn for the same model; only the meaning of
a has changed. On the left, every step in b drags a along with it, so the only
way down is a diagonal line. On the right, a and b can move independently.

This is the "ridge" row from Tuesday's table, and centering is its standard fix.
It applies to any covariate with a large offset from zero: year, elevation,
temperature in Kelvin, body mass in grams.
:::

# Fix 2: rescale

## Data that span orders of magnitude {.smaller}

**Are wide-ranging birds more likely to be long-distance migrants?** AVONET,
`r format(nrow(birds), big.mark = ",")` species. Range size runs from under 1 km² to
`r round(max(birds$Range.Size) / 1e6)` million km²; body mass from 2 g to 111 kg.

$$P(\text{migrant}) = \text{logistic}(a + b \cdot \text{range} + c \cdot \text{mass})$$

| Units | Nelder-Mead | BFGS |
|---|---|---|
| km² and grams, as in the data | NLL **`r format(round(fit_mig_nm$value), big.mark = ",")`**, `convergence` `r fit_mig_nm$convergence`, range effect the **wrong sign** | **error**: `non-finite finite-difference value` |
| millions of km², kg | `r format(round(fit_mig_sc_nm$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")` | `r format(round(fit_mig_sc$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")` |

. . .

**Same model.** In km², the range coefficient's right value is about 0.00000005. A
step that suits the intercept is ten million times too big for it.

::: {.notes}
The striking row is Nelder-Mead in raw units: an NLL more than twice the best,
reported as converged, with the range effect pointing the wrong way. A student
would have concluded that wide-ranging birds are less likely to migrate. The
right answer, from the rescaled fit and from glm(), is the opposite: migrants
have larger ranges, which makes sense, since a migrant's range includes both its
breeding and its wintering grounds.

Why it happens: an optimizer moves all parameters by steps of roughly similar
size. With range in km², multiplying a step of 0.1 in b by a range of 10 million
km² sends the log odds to a million, so every probability is 0 or 1 and the NLL
explodes. BFGS, estimating slopes from tiny nudges, gets an infinite slope and
stops with an error; Nelder-Mead shrinks its steps until it stops making
progress, somewhere wrong.

Not every model breaks this way: a straight-line model of hand-wing index against
the same raw range sizes fits fine, because nothing in it explodes. The trouble
comes when big raw values sit inside an exp() or a logistic, which is most of the
models in this course.
:::

## Your turn: change the units {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
mig_nll <- function(p, range, mass){
  prob <- plogis(p[1] + p[2] * range + p[3] * mass)
  -sum(dbinom(birds$migrant, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
}

fit_raw <- optim(c(0, 0, 0), mig_nll, range = birds$Range.Size, mass = birds$Mass)
fit_raw$par; fit_raw$value

fit_sc <- optim(c(0, 0, 0), mig_nll, range = birds$Range.Size / 1e6,
                mass = birds$Mass / 1000, method = "BFGS")
fit_sc$par; fit_sc$value
```
:::

**Check:** `r format(round(fit_mig_nm$value), big.mark = ",")` against
`r format(round(fit_mig_sc$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`. Which way does
the range effect point in each?

::: {.plain}
Choose units that put your covariates roughly between 0.1 and 100. The model is unchanged; only the numbers the optimizer handles get easier.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. Rescaling multiplies each coefficient by the same factor it divided
the covariate by, so the conclusions are identical: in millions of km², the range
coefficient is about 0.05 per million km² instead of 0.00000005 per km².

Two alternatives worth naming. optim()'s control = list(parscale = ...) tells it
the typical size of each parameter, and works without changing the data. And for
quantities that span orders of magnitude, a log scale is often better biology as
well as better numerics: log10 range and log10 mass fit these data noticeably
better than the raw versions. That is a different model, though, so it belongs
in a model comparison, not here.
:::

# Fix 3: keep parameters legal

## Three ways, in order of preference {.smaller}

| Fix | How | Where you have used it |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Transform** | fit the log of a positive parameter, the logit of a probability | Lecture 16's table; every `exp(log_k)` since |
| **2. Bound** | `method = "L-BFGS-B"` with `lower` and `upper` | Lecture 16's `size`; Tuesday's challenge |
| **3. Penalize** | return a huge NLL for an illegal value | Lecture 16's guard on the straight line |

. . .

Transforming is first because it **removes** the edge. Bounding stops at the edge.
A penalty builds a **cliff**, which is exactly what Tuesday warned about.

::: {.plain}
Rewrite the parameter so no value is illegal, if you can. Fence it in if you cannot. Punish it only as a last resort.
:::

::: {.notes}
A summary of things they have already done, ranked. The ranking is the new part,
and it is the one from the original version of this lecture.

The penalty's problem is Tuesday's "cliff" row: the surface jumps from a sensible
NLL to 1,000,000, so BFGS gets a meaningless slope near the edge. It works when
the answer is far from the edge, and quietly misbehaves when it is close.
:::

## Worked example: an unprotected fit {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

**Where on Florida's reefs do divers find the most fish species?** If richness
peaks at some intermediate depth, the hump from Tuesday describes it: how many
species at the peak, at what depth, and how fast richness falls away on either
side. Here with every parameter on its **natural** scale:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# p[1] peak richness, p[2] depth of the peak, p[3] width, p[4] negative binomial size
hump_nat <- function(p){
  mu <- p[1] * exp(-(reef$depth - p[2])^2 / (2 * p[3]^2))
  -sum(dnbinom(reef$richness, mu = mu, size = p[4], log = TRUE))
}

start <- c(25, 10, 20, 0.2)    # 25 species at 10 m, 20 m wide: a sensible guess
fit_nat <- optim(start, hump_nat, method = "BFGS")
fit_nat$value
fit_nat$par
```
:::

`r h_warn` warnings, `NaNs produced`. The answer: a peak of
**`r round(h_nat$par[1])` species at `r round(h_nat$par[2])` m**. The deepest
survey is at `r round(max(reef$depth))` m.

::: {.notes}
Biological context, if anyone asks why a hump: shallow reefs take the most
wave action and the biggest swings in temperature, while deeper reefs get less
light; somewhere between, there is often the most structure and the most kinds of
fish. Whether that is true here is what the model estimates, and on Tuesday it
put the peak near 16 m. Today the question is only whether the fit finds it.

Three minutes. Let the warnings scroll past, then ask them to read the
parameters: a hump centred hundreds of metres below the deepest dive is not a
description of these reefs.

What happened: on its way, BFGS tried a negative size and a negative peak. A
negative-binomial size below zero, or a negative expected count, is undefined, so
dnbinom() returned NaN, which is where the warnings come from. Those undefined
regions bent the search, and it ended somewhere absurd, with convergence 0.

The start is deliberately reasonable. Nothing about it signals trouble, which is
the point: protection is not something to add only when a start looks bad.
:::

## Fix it: transform {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Fit the **log** of everything that must be positive, then `exp()` it back:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
hump_log <- function(p){
  mu <- exp(p[1]) * exp(-(reef$depth - p[2])^2 / (2 * exp(p[3])^2))
  -sum(dnbinom(reef$richness, mu = mu, size = exp(p[4]), log = TRUE))
}

# the same start, on the log scale
fit_log <- optim(c(log(25), 10, log(20), log(0.2)), hump_log, method = "BFGS")
fit_log$value

# back to the natural scale: peak, depth, width, size
c(exp(fit_log$par[1]), fit_log$par[2], exp(fit_log$par[3]), exp(fit_log$par[4]))
```
:::

**Check:** NLL `r format(round(h_log$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`, a peak
of `r round(exp(h_log$par[1]), 1)` species at `r round(h_log$par[2], 1)` m. No warnings.

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Three exp() calls inside the function, and one line to
back-transform the answer: that is the whole fix. The depth of the peak stays on
its natural scale: it cannot be negative either, but the fit never comes near
the surface, so it needs no protection here. The bounds on the next slide do
protect it.

This is the "fit on a transformed scale, then back-transform" lesson from
Lecture 16, used for a different reason: there to keep a probability legal, here
to keep three positive parameters positive. Every value the optimizer can try is
now legal, so it never meets an NaN.
:::

## Fix it: bound {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Keep the natural scale, and fence each positive parameter in:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_bnd <- optim(start, hump_nat, method = "L-BFGS-B",
                 lower = c(peak  = 0.01,   # species at the peak: must be above 0
                           depth = 0,      # metres below the surface: not above it
                           width = 0.1,    # metres: must be above 0
                           size  = 0.01))  # clumping: must be above 0
fit_bnd$value
fit_bnd$par
```
:::

**Why these limits:** each sits just above zero, where the model stops making
sense, and far below any value the data would choose. The names are only labels,
to remind you which is which; the order is what matters.

**Check:** NLL `r format(round(h_bnd$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`, a peak
of `r round(h_bnd$par[1], 1)` species at `r round(h_bnd$par[2], 1)` m. No warnings,
and no back-transforming.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The same function as the unprotected fit, hump_nat, unchanged; the
protection is entirely in the call. method = "L-BFGS-B" is the one method that
accepts bounds.

Depth is measured in metres below the surface, so a peak above the water makes no
sense, and 0 is a natural limit for it. One nuance: that bound assumes richness
really does peak somewhere. If it simply fell with depth, the fit would push the
peak against the surface and stop on the bound. Here the peak is at 16 m, far
from it, but a fit sitting exactly on a bound always deserves a second look.

The other limits are small positive numbers rather than zero, because the search
can land exactly on a bound, and a size or width of exactly zero is still
undefined.
How small does not matter much, as long as it is well below anything plausible:
the best fit has a peak near 25 species, a width near 24 m and a size near 6.5,
so the limits are far out of its way.

The names in lower = c(peak = ...) are for the reader. optim() matches limits to
parameters by position, in the same order as the start vector, so the names do
not change anything, but they make a wrong order much easier to spot.

Bounds are a fine choice when you want the answer on its natural scale and there
is no natural transformation. Their weakness: the fit can end sitting on a
bound, which needs checking, as a plateau did in Lecture 19's challenge.
:::

## Fix it: penalize {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Return a huge NLL whenever a value is illegal:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
hump_pen <- function(p){
  if (any(p[c(1, 3, 4)] <= 0)) {     # peak, width or size not positive
    return(1e10)                     # a terrible score: go somewhere else
  }
  hump_nat(p)
}

fit_pen_bfgs <- optim(start, hump_pen, method = "BFGS")
fit_pen_nm   <- optim(start, hump_pen)                   # Nelder-Mead
fit_pen_bfgs$value; fit_pen_nm$value
```
:::

**Check:** BFGS puts the peak at **`r round(h_pen_bfgs$par[2])` m** again (NLL
`r format(round(h_pen_bfgs$value, 1), nsmall = 1, big.mark = ",")`). Nelder-Mead
finds **`r round(h_pen_nm$par[1], 1)` species at `r round(h_pen_nm$par[2], 1)` m**
(NLL `r format(round(h_pen_nm$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`), the same hump as
the transformed and bounded fits.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The if() is exactly the "cliff in the code" from Tuesday's table.
Below zero the NLL jumps from about 31,800 to 10,000,000,000.

BFGS estimates slopes by nudging each parameter a little. Near the edge, a
nudge either stays on the sensible side or falls off the cliff, so the slope it
computes is meaningless, and it ends where the unprotected fit did. Nelder-Mead
never computes a slope: it only compares values, and to it the cliff is simply a
region of very bad points to stay out of.

This is the guard students met in Lecture 16, on the straight-line occupancy
model, with a different number.
:::

## All three, side by side {.smaller}

| Protection | Method | NLL | Peak at |
|---|---|---|---|
| none | BFGS | `r format(round(h_nat$value, 1), nsmall = 1, big.mark = ",")` | `r round(h_nat$par[2])` m |
| **transform** | BFGS | **`r format(round(h_log$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`** | `r round(h_log$par[2], 1)` m |
| **bound** | L-BFGS-B | **`r format(round(h_bnd$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`** | `r round(h_bnd$par[2], 1)` m |
| penalize | BFGS | `r format(round(h_pen_bfgs$value, 1), nsmall = 1, big.mark = ",")` | `r round(h_pen_bfgs$par[2])` m |
| penalize | Nelder-Mead | `r format(round(h_pen_nm$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")` | `r round(h_pen_nm$par[2], 1)` m |

::: {.plain}
Transform first. Bounds also work. A penalty only works with a method that does not rely on slopes.
:::

::: {.notes}
The ranking on the earlier table, now with numbers behind it. Transforming and
bounding both work with any method; the penalty depends on choosing a method
that can cope with a cliff.

One caution worth saying: protection stops illegal values, it does not rescue a
bad start. From a start with a width of 2 m, all three protected fits still go
wrong. That is Fix 4.
:::

# When one fit fails

## A loop that dies on one bad fit {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Lecture 16's straight line, unguarded, from ten random starts:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
lin_nll <- function(p){
  prob <- p[1] + p[2] * occ$elapsed
  -sum(dbinom(occ$n_occupied, size = occ$n_routes, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
}

set.seed(20)
results <- rep(NA, 10)
for (i in 1:10) {                      # this loop fails on purpose
  start <- c(runif(1, 0.5, 1), runif(1, -0.03, 0.01))
  results[i] <- optim(start, lin_nll, method = "BFGS")$value
}
results
```
:::

It stops at fit **`r first_error`** with `initial value in 'vmmin' is not finite`.
One impossible start ends the whole loop.

::: {.notes}
Some starts put a probability above 1 for some year, so the NLL is not a number
and BFGS refuses to begin. In a loop, that error does not just lose one fit: it
stops everything after it, and results holds only what came before.

Students will meet this in Part 2 of the assignment the first time they loop over
starting values or profile a parameter.
:::

## `tryCatch()`: record the failure, keep going {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(20)
results <- rep(NA, 10)
for (i in 1:10) {
  start <- c(runif(1, 0.5, 1), runif(1, -0.03, 0.01))
  results[i] <- tryCatch(
    optim(start, lin_nll, method = "BFGS")$value,
    error = function(e){ NA }               # if it fails, record NA
  )
}
results
```
:::

**`r sum(!is.na(loop_res))` of 10** fits succeed; the failures are `NA`, and the
loop finishes.

::: {.plain}
tryCatch() says: try this, and if it throws an error, do this instead.
:::

::: {.notes}
tryCatch() runs the first expression; if it raises an error, it runs the error
function instead and returns that function's value, here NA. The loop never sees
the error.

Worth adding: the NA rows are information. If most starts fail, the problem is
the model (here, a model that can propose impossible probabilities), not bad
luck. The fix for this particular model is Fix 3, a transformation.
:::

## Errors, warnings, and `try()` {.smaller}

An **error** stops your code. A **warning** prints a message and carries on.

| | What it does |
|---|---|
| `try(code, silent = TRUE)` | runs the code; if it fails, returns a `"try-error"` object instead of stopping |
| `tryCatch(code, error = ..., warning = ...)` | lets you choose what happens on an error, on a warning, or both |

`try()` is the quick version:

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit <- try(optim(start, lin_nll, method = "BFGS"), silent = TRUE)
if (inherits(fit, "try-error")) {
  cat("this start failed\n")
}
```

::: {.notes}
Two slides, and not ones to type: a reference for when they need it.

The distinction worth making explicit: errors and warnings are different things.
An error ends the computation. A warning, such as the NaNs produced messages from
the unprotected hump earlier, lets it finish, which is why warnings are so easy
to ignore and why it is worth reading them.

try() needs only one function, and inherits(x, "try-error") to test whether it
worked.

These tools are not only for model fitting. Any loop over many things that can
fail individually, such as reading a folder of files or downloading from an
API, uses the same pattern, and students will meet it in their own projects.
:::

## `tryCatch()`, and a caution {.smaller}

`tryCatch()` is the flexible version: a separate response for errors and for
warnings, and `finally =` for code that must run either way.

```{r}
#| eval: false
result <- tryCatch(
  optim(start, lin_nll, method = "BFGS")$value,
  error = function(e){
    message("failed: ", conditionMessage(e))   # record WHY it failed
    NA
  }
)
```

::: {.plain}
Catching an error hides it. Keep a record of what failed, and if most attempts fail, fix the model rather than the loop.
:::

::: {.notes}
finally = is for clean-up, such as closing a file or a connection, that has to
happen whether the code worked or not.

The caution is the important part. tryCatch() makes a loop finish, but it also
makes failures silent unless you record them. conditionMessage(e) gives the
error's text, so it can be saved alongside the NA. If most attempts fail, the
problem is the model, as it was with the unguarded straight line, and the fix is
Fix 3, not a better loop.
:::

# Fix 4: good starting values

## Where starting values come from {.smaller}

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| **The plot** | read the reef peak off the graph: about 25 species at about 15 m |
| **A simpler model** | fit the nested model first; start the bigger one from its estimates |
| **A rough calculation** | method of moments, Lecture 15 |
| **A coarse grid** | for one or two parameters, Tuesday's brute force |

::: {.notes}
The first is the most underused. A start that is merely in the right
neighborhood rules out most false bottoms, and the plot gives that for free.

The second is the most powerful, and the next slide shows why: a nested model is
the bigger model with something fixed, so its fit is a point on the bigger
model's surface that is already good.
:::

## Build up from the simpler model {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

**Does development hurt bobwhite only past a threshold?** Tuesday's challenge:
counts stay flat until a route is a fraction $t$ developed, then fall. From
Tuesday's start, `optim()` slid to $t$ below zero, which means **no threshold at
all**. Two models, one nested in the other:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
plain_nll <- function(p){            # counts fall from the first development
  mu <- exp(p[1] + p[2] * counts$frac_built)
  -sum(dnbinom(counts$count, mu = mu, size = exp(p[3]), log = TRUE))
}
threshold_nll <- function(p){        # counts flat until a fraction p[3] is built
  mu <- exp(p[1] + p[2] * pmax(0, counts$frac_built - p[3]))
  -sum(dnbinom(counts$count, mu = mu, size = exp(p[4]), log = TRUE))
}
```
:::

With $t = 0$, the threshold model **is** the plain model.

::: {.notes}
The biology first, because the fitting trick only makes sense once the two
models are clear. The plain model says development costs bobwhite from the very
first house. The threshold model says there is some level of development they
tolerate, and only beyond it do counts fall. Which is right matters for
management: a threshold would mean there is a safe amount of development.

Nested: set the threshold to zero and pmax(0, u - 0) is just u, so the threshold
model collapses to the plain one. That is what the next slide uses.
:::

## Start from the plain fit {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_plain <- optim(c(2, -1, 0), plain_nll)

# start exactly at the plain model: its estimates, with a threshold of 0
fit_built <- optim(c(fit_plain$par[1:2], 0, fit_plain$par[3]), threshold_nll)

fit_built$par[3]              # the threshold: fraction of the route developed
exp(fit_built$par[1])         # expected bobwhite on a route below the threshold
fit_built$value
```
:::

**Check:** a threshold of **`r round(100 * fit_built$par[3], 1)`%** developed, with
about **`r round(exp(fit_built$par[1]), 1)`** bobwhite expected on a route below it
(NLL `r format(round(fit_built$value, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`, the best
possible). Tuesday's start stopped at a threshold of
`r round(fit_tuesday$par[3], 2)`: no threshold at all.

. . .

The biology: there is a threshold, but it is **so close to zero** that there is
effectively no safe level of development.

::: {.notes}
The idea: the plain model's estimates are a point on the threshold model's
surface that is already as good as the plain model, and on the right side of it.
From there, Nelder-Mead walks straight into the dip that Tuesday's start missed.

exp() on the first parameter turns the log of the expected count back into
birds, the back-transforming habit from Lecture 16.

This is a general strategy for Part 2 of the assignment: fit the simplest
version, then add one piece at a time, each starting from the last fit.
:::

## What to try, in order {.smaller}

| You see | Likely cause | Try |
|---|---|---|
| an error before it starts | a start that is illegal | a legal start; transform (Fix 3) |
| estimates that disagree between starts | false bottoms | more starts; build up (Fix 4) |
| estimates strongly correlated | a ridge | center (Fix 1) |
| coefficients differing a hundredfold | scales | rescale (Fix 2) |
| a curve that misses the data | any of the above | draw it, then work up this table |
| one failure stops a loop | | `tryCatch()` |

::: {.notes}
The summary to photograph for the assignment. Read it alongside Tuesday's
checklist: that one says how to notice a problem, this one what to do about it.

The correlation between estimates is easy to get from mle2: cov2cor(vcov(fit)).
Anything beyond about 0.9 in absolute value is worth centering for.
:::

# Challenge

## Challenge: fix this model {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Reef richness against depth, $\text{depth}^2$, visibility and year, written the way
data usually arrive:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
bad_nll <- function(p){
  mu <- exp(p[1] + p[2] * reef$depth + p[3] * reef$depth^2 +
            p[4] * reef$visibility + p[5] * reef$year)
  -sum(dnbinom(reef$richness, mu = mu, size = p[6], log = TRUE))
}

start <- c(3, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1)
first_try <- optim(start, bad_nll, method = "BFGS")
first_try$value
first_try$convergence
```
:::

**Get the lowest NLL you can.** Same data, same model: change only how it is
written. Note what you changed.

::: {.notes}
Fifteen minutes, in pairs. The first try gives about
`r format(round(fx_raw), big.mark = ",")`, with convergence 0. The best possible
is `r format(round(fx_glm, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`. Keep a running best
on the board, with what each pair changed.

The changes allowed are the ones from today: what the covariates are measured
from (centering), what units they are in (rescaling), and how size is written
(transforming). The model itself, its curve and its distribution, stays the same,
which is what makes the NLLs comparable.

Hints for anyone stuck after five minutes, in order:

1. Today's table. Which rows describe this model?
2. What is year measured from, here? And what does depth squared run up to?
3. One fix alone is not enough.

Do not reveal the next slide until the board settles.
:::

## How the room could have won {.smaller}

| The model with... | BFGS reaches |
|---|---|
| nothing changed | `r format(round(fx_raw, 1), nsmall = 1, big.mark = ",")` |
| nothing changed, Nelder-Mead instead | `r format(round(fx_nm, 1), nsmall = 1, big.mark = ",")` |
| **only** year centered | `r format(round(fx_center, 1), nsmall = 1, big.mark = ",")` |
| **only** depth and visibility rescaled | `r format(round(fx_scale, 1), nsmall = 1, big.mark = ",")` |
| year centered **and** depth and visibility rescaled | **`r format(round(fx_both, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`** |

. . .

**One fix alone is not enough. Together, they reach the bottom.** And a
completely different fitting routine, `MASS::glm.nb()`, agrees to the second
decimal: `r format(round(fx_glm, 2), nsmall = 2, big.mark = ",")`.

::: {.plain}
Most failed fits have more than one cause. Fix what you can find, then check the answer a second, independent way.
:::

::: {.notes}
The model has two independent problems: a ridge from the calendar year (2014 to
2024, so the intercept is in year 0 AD), and badly matched scales from depth in
metres with depth squared running to 1,000. The second is why the Assignment 3
starter script divides depth by 10 for Part 1c. Fixing either alone leaves the other
to stall BFGS. Fixing both makes it easy.

Nelder-Mead does better on the unfixed model than BFGS does, but still stops
short: a reminder that switching method can paper over a badly written model
without curing it.

glm.nb() is a preview of Lecture 24: it fits this kind of model with a
specialized algorithm, and it makes a good independent check on a hand-written
NLL when the model happens to be one it can fit.

Deliberately no interpretation of the coefficients here: this is close to
Assignment 3's Part 1c, and the point of the exercise is the fitting.
:::
